items.title: [esa.int] Hubble and Webb expose hidden structures in Carina star-forming cloud
items.content_html:
🔭 ✏️

NASA’s Hubble and James Webb space telescopes have captured complementary views of the Cat’s Head Nebula, a star-forming pillar in the Carina Nebula about 7,500 light-years from Earth. Hubble’s visible-light image shows a dark dust column edged by glowing gas, while Webb’s infrared observations reveal details within the dust, including stars and fine strands. The images, released Oct. 29, help astronomers examine how young stars form in gas and dust exposed to radiation from massive nearby stars. Ultraviolet radiation and stellar winds likely shaped the pillar’s outline by eroding its surroundings, while denser material resisted erosion. Webb also imaged the lower-metallicity N159 star-forming region in the Large Magellanic Cloud, while Chandra and Webb observations show young stars forming in a separate Carina cloud.

items.title: [phys.org] Extra schooling under UK reform linked to fewer dementia diagnoses
items.content_html:
🔭 ✏️

A study of more than 100,000 UK Biobank participants found that a 1972 British law requiring teenagers to stay in school until 16 was associated with fewer diagnoses of Alzheimer’s disease and related dementias nearly 50 years later. Using the reform’s September 1, 1957, birth-date cutoff, researchers compared people subject to different school-leaving rules and reported a 0.88% reduction in dementia incidence among those affected. Researchers also found the reduction among participants with high genetic susceptibility. They cautioned that dementia was uncommon in this cohort, whose diagnoses were tracked only through age 65, making the estimate imprecise. Continued follow-up will help determine whether the difference persists as participants age.

items.title: [phys.org] Researchers document sustained sexual bond between Ethiopian bull and male donkey
items.content_html:
🔭 ✏️

An Italian-led research team documented repeated sexual interactions between a bull and a male donkey on an Ethiopian plateau, describing a selective social bond between the animals. During eight days of observation in March 2026, the bull, Achilles, mounted the donkey, Patroclus, 51 times; 34 mountings involved penetration. The findings appeared Nov. 2 in the journal Current Biology. The pair also licked, rubbed and nuzzled one another, and researchers repeatedly saw them seek each other out despite access to other potential mates. The team cautions that observations of one domesticated pair cannot establish why the behavior occurred or what the animals felt. Dry-season conditions led herders to move them to separate pastures; researchers in Ethiopia are trying to arrange a reunion to observe whether their interactions resume.

items.title: [discovermagazine.com] Tests find coca and alcohol in Inca child mummies, but none of the hallucinogens screened for
items.content_html:
🔭 ✏️

Researchers analyzing hair and nails from eight Inca children sacrificed about 500 years ago found traces of coca in hair and evidence of alcohol in some children, but none of the hallucinogens they tested for. The remains came from mountain sites in Peru and Argentina and belonged to children aged 6 to 14. The findings suggest the substances may have helped prepare children for the physical and emotional strain of journeys to sacrificial sites rather than induce hallucinations, said archaeologist Dagmara Socha of the University of Warsaw. Harmine, a plant compound associated with Amazonian species, was found in a nail from Juanita, a 14-year-old mummy. The team plans further study of the substances and sacred mountain sites.

items.title: [space.com] Rubin observatory team finds possible dwarf planet in archived images
items.content_html:
🔭 ✏️

A team led by University of Washington astronomer Mario Juric has identified a possible dwarf planet in early data from Chile’s Vera C. Rubin Observatory and estimates it is 1,000 to 2,000 miles across. The object, provisionally designated 2026 ED-138, lies about 46 astronomical units from Earth; the team also found it in older observations, including photographic plates dating to the 1930s. The estimated size would make it far larger than the asteroids the survey team usually detects, but astronomers have not established that it is round, a requirement for dwarf-planet status. Because it is too distant for researchers to image its shape directly, they plan to study how it dims stars as it passes in front of them; one such event may occur within days, Juric said. He expects confirmation to take about two years.

items.title: [abcnews.com] Swift telescope shutdown ends rapid alerts for cosmic explosions
items.content_html:
🔭 ✏️

NASA shut down its Swift Observatory in late October after it could no longer hold steady enough for observations, ending a 22-year mission to detect gamma-ray bursts, supernovas and other high-energy events. Swift’s rapid observations helped direct other space telescopes toward eruptions for more detailed study, and astronomers are working out how to replace that alert function. The observatory resumed observations after the rescue effort ended and captured additional gamma-ray bursts and other ultrahigh-energy events before NASA turned off its systems. Over its mission, Swift recorded more than 2,000 gamma-ray bursts and 1,400 exploding stars.

items.title: [scitechdaily.com] Study suggests Neptune formed from materials that originated closer to the young Sun
items.content_html:
🔭 ✏️

Neptune may have formed from building blocks that originated closer to the young Sun before moving outward, according to research published in Astronomy & Astrophysics. Neptune’s deep atmosphere appears considerably richer in oxygen than Uranus’s, despite the planets’ similar size and mass, suggesting different chemical histories. Researchers used carbon monoxide measurements and atmospheric models to infer the planets’ hidden chemistry; they cannot directly sample the deep atmospheres. The proposed formation pathway therefore depends on models. Future spacecraft observations or atmospheric probes could help test it. NASA’s planned Uranus Orbiter and Probe is expected to launch sometime in the next decade.

items.title: [theguardian.com] UN-backed report warns overshooting 1.5C could permanently damage Earth's ice
items.content_html:
🔭 ✏️

A report by 80 scientists convened by the International Cryosphere Climate Initiative and the U.N. Environment Programme warns that even a temporary rise above the Paris Agreement’s 1.5C warming limit could cause lasting losses to glaciers, sea ice and polar ice sheets. Earth has already warmed about 1.3C from preindustrial levels. The authors say any period above 1.5C should be as brief as possible before temperatures fall much further, and identify a long-term target below 1C by 2150. Under current policies, warming is projected to reach about 2.8C, a level the report links to near-total thaw of near-surface permafrost and likely severe disruption to ocean circulation. Greenland and Antarctic ice sheets would continue losing ice even if temperatures later returned to 1.5C, while many ice systems could take centuries or millennia to recover. The report was released ahead of the COP31 climate conference in Turkey.

🔭 ✏️

The exceptionally strong El Niño developing in the tropical Pacific is intensifying weather risks across several regions, including heavy rain and flash floods in the U.S. Southwest. Scientists say the pattern adds moisture to the air and shifts winds, making downpours more likely, although it is not the sole cause of individual storms. The World Meteorological Organization expects the event to peak in December and persist into February 2027. The agency says it could rank among the strongest since at least 1950. Flooding has also been reported in Peru and Ecuador, while Indonesia and parts of Southeast Asia are unusually dry. In the Southwest, flooding prompted evacuations, and the San Juan River threatened Pagosa Springs, Colorado. Warmer oceans linked to human-caused climate change may amplify the event’s effects, but scientists caution that separating El Niño’s contribution from the long-term warming trend remains difficult. In September, sea-surface temperature in the Pacific’s Niño 3.4 reference region reached 29.70°C, while the global ocean average for that month, excluding polar waters, set a September record of 21.05°C. Forecasters expect the strongest effects to continue into 2027.

items.title: [news.un.org] UN says record greenhouse gases lock in centuries-long warming
items.content_html:
🔭 ✏️

The World Meteorological Organization (WMO), the United Nations’ weather agency, reported that atmospheric concentrations of carbon dioxide, methane and nitrous oxide all reached record levels in 2025. Carbon dioxide averaged 426.8 parts per million, methane 1,948 parts per billion and nitrous oxide 339.1 parts per billion—153%, 267% and 126% of pre-industrial levels, respectively. The annual bulletin measures gases accumulated in the atmosphere, not emissions released during the year. About half of annual carbon dioxide emissions remain in the atmosphere. The WMO says the gases’ heat-trapping effect will drive warming for decades or centuries; the past 11 years were the warmest on record. Carbon dioxide rose 2.8 parts per million from 2024 to 2025, below the previous year’s 3.6-ppm increase but still above the decade average of 2.6 ppm. The WMO linked the slower increase partly to recovering land carbon sinks and fewer fire emissions after the 2023-24 El Niño. It warned that concentrations could rise further in 2026 as fossil-fuel use continues and another powerful El Niño affects land sinks. The bulletin will inform negotiators at the Nov. 9-20 COP31 climate summit in Antalya, Türkiye.

items.content_html:

Heat-related disruption cost the world an estimated $1.07 trillion in lost worker productivity in 2025, while extreme drought affected about 52% of global land for at least a month, according to the 2026 Lancet Countdown report. The report’s 146 researchers from 30 countries urged governments to treat climate change as a global health emergency and coordinate a sustained response. Extreme rainfall affected 17.2% of global land each year from 2016 to 2025, up from 14.8% in the preceding decade, and the researchers linked shifting groundwater conditions to risks for food security and sanitation. Southeast Asia and Africa suffered the largest productivity-related economic losses, equivalent to 3.9% and 3.2% of gross domestic product, respectively. Clean-energy investment reached $2.1 trillion in 2025, nearly twice fossil-fuel investment, but fossil fuels still supplied more than 80% of global energy. The report calls for governments to consider health in climate decisions and direct climate and health funding to vulnerable countries. Researchers are expected to press the issue at the COP31 climate conference in Antalya, Türkiye, scheduled for Nov. 9-20.

items.title: [space.com] NASA Swift telescope faces uncontrolled reentry after failed orbit rescue
items.content_html:
🔭 ✏️

NASA’s Neil Gehrels Swift Observatory is expected to reenter Earth’s atmosphere in the coming days after a failed attempt to raise its orbit. Forecasts place reentry roughly between Nov. 3 and Nov. 6, but the timing and location remain uncertain. The U.S. Space Force is tracking the 1.5-ton spacecraft. Most of it is expected to burn up, although some dense tungsten components and mirror parts could survive. The possible reentry corridor spans a broad band near the equator, much of it over ocean. Solar activity increased atmospheric drag and accelerated the telescope’s orbital decline. Swift, launched in 2004 for a two-year mission, detected more than 2,000 gamma-ray bursts and 1,400 exploding stars and rapidly alerted other observatories to transient events. It continued observations after the rescue attempt was abandoned, but NASA shut down its systems in late October when its low orbit made stable operations impossible.

items.title: [cloud.google.com] Google bans Chinese partner after backdoor infects 1.3 million Android boxes
items.content_html:
🔭 ✏️

Google and security partners disrupted the XCPE botnet, which had enrolled more than 1.3 million Android devices, mostly TV set-top boxes. Google says it has high confidence that Shenzhen-based manufacturer Videostrong Technology Co. deliberately embedded the backdoor in device firmware and sold criminal groups access to infected hardware. The criminal groups used the devices to commit advertising fraud, route other people’s internet traffic through household connections and install additional malware. Google also reported that operators captured screens, collected account information and system logs, and issued commands remotely. The same malware appeared on telehealth equipment, karaoke machines and digital signs. Google’s takedown targeted XCPE control servers and domains used by more than a dozen related malware families. Google estimates the takedown could also cut criminal access to at least 10 million other devices compromised through separate routes. Videostrong evaded Google’s device checks by loading malicious code after a device’s first boot, Google said. Google has banned Videostrong and its future affiliates from making certified Android devices or supplying software to certified manufacturers, and says it changed its review process. The backdoor remains in affected devices and can reinstall after a reboot. Synthient, a security firm involved in the investigation, recommends disconnecting and replacing affected boxes.

items.title: [blog.ovhcloud.com] PHP hosting provider backports fixes across six million sites as patching lags
items.content_html:
🔭 ✏️

Hosting provider OVHcloud says it deployed official fixes or its own backports across all 15 PHP versions on its shared-hosting platform, covering more than 6 million websites on about 5,000 servers. The fixes address two PHP flaws collectively known as PHP2Shell that can let attackers run commands on vulnerable servers without credentials. The U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) has confirmed active exploitation and set an Oct. 29 deadline for federal civilian agencies to address the flaws. Censys’ tracker showed more than 10 million services patched since Oct. 21, while a scan found more than 4 million services in Germany still reporting vulnerable PHP version numbers. The scanner cautions that backported fixes may not appear in those version strings. OVHcloud says it wrote fixes for PHP 5.3 through 7.3, versions the PHP project no longer maintains. Researchers documented 35 shell executions on three deliberately vulnerable honeypots, but the test used a favorable single-worker setup. CISA has not named affected organizations or described the evidence behind its listing, and the designation does not establish the scale of successful compromises in production. Some earlier claims of successful exploitation were withdrawn or qualified after investigators found scanning or could not confirm PHP2Shell as the entry point.

items.title: [reuters.com] European supermarkets hit by attacks on refrigeration controls
items.content_html:
🔭 ✏️

Attackers switched supermarket refrigeration units’ evaporators into defrost mode in Belgium on Nov. 2, refrigeration operator Sabcobel said, while investigators and retailers assessed similar incidents across several countries. Some affected equipment used temperature-control technology from Danish manufacturer Danfoss, whose technology was also involved in the October attack on French stores. Officials have not established who was behind the latest incidents or whether the events were linked. Sweden’s National Cybersecurity Centre said it had identified many internet-exposed operational-technology devices that needed updates or patches, while cybersecurity researcher Kevin Beaumont said some refrigeration controllers remained reachable online after the French attack. Sabcobel chief executive Stephan Moelans said affected units had to be disconnected and that full protection required physical modifications as well as software updates. A secure internet connection was an interim measure, he said.

items.title: [sootoday.com] Canada and EU set health, minerals agenda for Montreal summit
items.content_html:
🔭 ✏️

Canada and the European Union are planning closer cooperation on pandemic readiness and critical-mineral investment at their Oct. 29-30 summit in Montreal. European Crisis Management Commissioner Hadja Lahbib said the partners plan joint emergency-response stress tests and closer coordination on vaccine research and supplies. The European Investment Bank is also expected to sign a framework agreement to support investment in Canadian critical-mineral projects. Prime Minister Mark Carney said the summit will launch formal negotiations on a deeper partnership over the following year, covering trade, defence, energy, technology and research. Lahbib said the health cooperation aims to secure supplies and reduce reliance on less predictable partners. The Quebec government has criticized Ottawa for denying Premier Paul St-Pierre Plamondon a speaking role and refusing to let the province host a reception. Carney said the premier was invited to a dinner with European officials and that federal representatives had held three consultations with Quebec about the negotiations.
